hookLine: two great teachers read prajnanam brahma two ways

lines: IS THE KNOWING IN ME BRAHMAN?
cards: Two people read the same text message and come away sure of opposite things. Same words, same punctuation, and a whole evening of argument about what the sender meant.
The Aitareya's great saying has had that kind of evening for a very long time. Prajnanam brahma: the knowing is Brahman. So is the knowing in me Brahman?
Two great teachers of Vedanta read the very same two Sanskrit words, and land in different places.

teach.b: Shankara, the teacher of Advaita, reads it straight. The knowing in a person and Brahman are one, without a second.
What feels like a separate knower, a small self with its own little light, is a misreading. When it's seen through, nothing new is gained; the knowing was Brahman all along.
His strongest point: the Aitareya walks back from the thing, to the sense, to the knowing, and then simply says, the knowing is Brahman. Not is like. Not lives in.
Is. Ramanuja reads the same words another way.

For him, the self that knows is real and distinct, and Brahman dwells within it as its inner ruler, the self of the self. Saying the knowing is Brahman is true the way pointing at a body names the person living in it.

teach.h: A REAL KNOWER, TO KNOW AND TO LOVE.
teach.b: His strongest point: the Upanishads also speak of Brahman as the inner controller who dwells within all beings, and as the Lord to be loved; a real knower remains, to know and to love.
Both teachers hold the Upanishad as true. Both read it closely. In Sanskrit the saying is just two words side by side, with no is between them; English supplies it.
The teachers part over what that missing is is doing: the same as, or the indwelling of. Both readings are still taught, each with its own teachers and its own devotion.
The Aitareya doesn't settle it for them, and this lesson doesn't either.

how: Students in each Vedanta school study the great sayings through their own school's commentaries, so prajnanam brahma is taught with Shankara as the guide in Advaita and with Ramanuja in Sri Vaishnava communities.

o: four great sayings that name the self as Brahman
four names for the gods in the oldest hymns
four debates between rival schools of Vedanta

games.q: two readings of one saying. tap the pairs.
p: the knowing and Brahman: one, no second
Brahman as the knower's inner ruler

s: in Vedanta, everyone reads prajnanam brahma the same way
Shankara reads one without a second; Ramanuja reads Brahman dwelling within a real, distinct knower.
Ramanuja treats the Upanishads as less true than Shankara does
both hold the text as true and read it closely; they differ on what 'is' means.
for Shankara, the separate knower is a misreading that gets seen through
nothing new is gained when it's seen through; the knowing was Brahman all along.

games.q: your study partner reads prajnanam brahma Shankara's way and asks you for the other side's best case. what do you give?
o: the Upanishads also call Brahman the inner ruler within beings; a real knower remains to love.
Ramanuja simply didn't read the Sanskrit as carefully as Shankara did.
the other side says the saying is only poetry and makes no claim.
games.why: Ramanuja reads the same line closely: Brahman dwells within a real, distinct self as its inner ruler, the self of the self. Both readings are still taught.

practice: On a scrap of paper, write the saying twice. Once as Shankara hears it: the knowing is Brahman, one without a second. Once as Ramanuja hears it: Brahman dwells within the knower as its inner self.
Read both lines slowly, and stay longest with the one you didn't expect to like.

wordCard.voice: The four mahavakyas, and prajnanam brahma heard two ways: one without a second, or Brahman dwelling within the one who knows.

orig.note: Sanskrit prajnanam brahma, the knowing is Brahman: the Aitareya's great saying, read in more than one way.

carryVoice: Here's the line: one with Brahman, or Brahman dwelling within. One saying, two careful readings. Day 1739, done.

sources.ref: Shankara, commentary on the Aitareya Upanishad (the saying read as identity; the separate knower as a superimposition removed by knowledge)
Ramanuja, Vedartha Sangraha and Sri Bhashya (Brahman as the inner self and ruler of real, distinct selves; the great sayings read accordingly); Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.7 (the inner controller)
